input: Sign up for an improv comedy writing workshop

keyUnknowns.whyItMatters: Improv and comedy writing can overlap but are distinct disciplines — knowing whether the user wants performance-based improv, written comedy craft, or a hybrid changes which workshops to target.
Whether the user wants an in-person local class or an online workshop drastically changes the search and registration process.
Workshops vary from single-day intensives to multi-week courses — knowing how much time the user can commit narrows the options significantly.
Workshop costs range from free community sessions to several-hundred-dollar professional programs; the budget determines which options are realistic.
Knowing the user's experience level (total beginner vs. some improv or writing background) determines whether to look for beginner, intermediate, or open-level workshops.
The user may have a preference for a specific focus — e.g., sketch comedy, stand-up, sitcom writing, or pure stage improv — which shapes which programs are the best fit.
Understanding what the user hopes to get out of the workshop (a fun hobby experience, networking, a credential, or professional development) determines what 'the right workshop' actually looks like.

gold.taskTitle: Sign up for an improv comedy writing workshop
gold.taskDescription: Find and register for an improv comedy writing workshop that fits the user's needs.

questions.title: Is this more about improv performance or comedy writing craft?
questions.description: Clarify whether the user is primarily interested in stage improv (performance, games, scenes), written comedy (sketch, sitcom, stand-up scripts), or a workshop that genuinely blends both.

questions.title: Do you want an in-person class or is online fine?
questions.description: Determine whether the user needs a local, in-person workshop or is open to virtual options, which defines the entire search geography.

questions.title: How much time can you commit to this workshop?
questions.description: Find out if the user is looking for a one-day intensive, a weekend retreat, or a multi-week ongoing course.

questions.title: What is your budget for the workshop fee?
questions.description: Establish a price range the user is comfortable with, from free community events up to professional program tuition.

questions.title: What is your current experience level with improv or comedy?
questions.description: Determine if the user is a complete beginner, has done some recreational improv or writing, or has more serious prior training.

questions.title: Is there a specific comedy style or format you want to focus on?
questions.description: Find out if the user has a preference for a particular form — sketch, stand-up, long-form improv, sitcom writing, etc. — to target the most relevant programs.

questions.title: What do you most want to walk away with after the workshop?
questions.description: Understand the user's primary goal — e.g., a fun new hobby, usable written material, professional skills, or meeting like-minded people — to define what success looks like.
